Sup A: kontoravdi_2005 · Kontoravdi et al. (2005) CHO growth and mAb model
This model describes hybridoma cell cultures that produce IgG1 monoclonal antibody, predicting viable and total cell concentrations, nutrient and metabolite levels, and antibody concentration in the culture medium. It combines a population-level description of cell growth, death, nutrient use, and metabolite formation with intracellular steps for antibody synthesis, assembly, processing, and secretion. The model was developed from batch-culture data and then its sensitive parameters were estimated using data from an optimally designed fed-batch experiment. The cultures were run in Erlenmeyer flasks, with concentrated glucose and glutamine feed added in pulses. Its predictions were checked against a separate fed-batch experiment, with good overall agreement but some mismatch in late-culture viability predictions. The paper presents the model-development method as a way to support in-silico experimentation, control, and optimisation while limiting experimental work.
antibody: The antibody mechanism represents heavy- and light-chain gene transcription and translation, sequential assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum, transport to the Golgi, and secretion into the medium.
application: The authors propose using the resulting model for in-silico experimentation and model-based control and optimisation.
batch fit: In batch cultures, the model reproduced the viable-cell peak and antibody concentration profiles and showed similar agreement for the measured nutrients and metabolites.
cell death: The model makes the specific cell-death rate dependent on extracellular ammonia.
cell line: The cultures used HFN7.1 hybridoma cells producing IgG1 against human-plasma fibronectin.
equipment: Batch and fed-batch cultures were run in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks with a 200 mL working volume.
estimation: Parameter estimation used maximum likelihood, constant-variance measurement errors, and the SRQPD sequential quadratic programming code in gPROMS.
experimental design: The design was implemented in gPROMS using its experiment-design-for-parameter-precision function and an SRQPD sequential quadratic programming code.
experimental design: The designed experiment lasted 168 h, with a daily feed pulse at 24 h intervals.
experimental design: The fed-batch experiment was designed using a D-optimal criterion to maximise information for estimating the seven selected parameters.
fed-batch fit: For the designed fed-batch experiment, the model closely tracked glutamine and antibody concentrations and captured the overall profiles of the measured variables.
feeding: Batch cultures began at 29.1 mM glucose and 4.9 mM glutamine.
feeding: The concentrated feed contained 500 mM glucose and 100 mM glutamine.
feeding: The designed experiment used one feed pulse per day, whereas the independent experiment used two doses per day.
feeding: The designed fed-batch experiment began at 25.1 mM glucose and 5.01 mM glutamine.
feeding: The independent fed-batch experiment began at 18.4 mM glucose and 3.74 mM glutamine.
feeding: The maximum total feed volume was 8.75 mL, less than 5% of the 200 mL culture volume.
growth: Cell growth depends on glucose and glutamine availability and on extracellular lactate and ammonia accumulation, with growth described using Monod kinetics.
inoculation: The cultures were inoculated at 2 × 10^8 cells/L.
limitations: In the designed fed-batch experiment, the model predicted faster use of newly supplied glutamine than the measurements showed after glutamine had reached zero.
limitations: In the final 40 h of the designed fed-batch experiment, the model overpredicted viable-cell concentration.
measurements: Cell density was measured with a hemacytometer and viability was determined by Trypan Blue dye exclusion.
measurements: Extracellular antibody concentration was measured by indirect sandwich ELISA, with absorbance read at 450 nm.
measurements: Extracellular glucose, glutamine, lactate, and ammonia were measured with a YSI Bioprofiler 200.
medium: The basal medium was high-glucose DMEM at 4.5 g/L supplemented with 2.5% bovine calf serum.
metabolism: The model represents glucose and glutamine uptake, glutamine degradation, lactate production, and ammonia production.
model form: The model comprises 28 differential and algebraic equations and 30 parameters.
model form: The model is described as a hybrid structured/unstructured model of antibody-secreting hybridoma cultures.
operation: Culture temperature and carbon-dioxide concentration were automatically controlled at 37°C and 5%, respectively.
outputs: The model describes cell growth and antibody synthesis and production alongside extracellular culture variables.
parameterisation: Batch-culture data provided initial estimates for parameters targeted for estimation because cell growth and product synthesis and secretion parameters were considered cell-line-specific.
prior work: The model structure was presented previously by Kontoravdi et al. 2005 and compared with data for the 14-4-4S hybridoma cell line.
replicates: Batch cultures were conducted in triplicate flasks, while fed-batch cultures were conducted in duplicate flasks.
sampling: At each sampling point, viable and total cell, nutrient, metabolite, and extracellular antibody concentrations were determined in the independent fed-batch experiment.
sampling: For the fed-batch design, the earliest sample was set at 12 h and the minimum interval between measurements was 6 h.
sensitivity: A one-at-a-time screening was used to identify parameters influencing the other measured outputs, and seven parameters were selected for estimation.
sensitivity: The authors used Sobol' global sensitivity analysis to assess how parameter variation affected predicted antibody concentration.
uncertainty: The 95% confidence intervals were within ±10% of final estimates for all selected parameters except the ammonia yield, whose interval was ±17%.
validation: In the independent fed-batch experiment, the model correctly estimated the final extracellular monoclonal-antibody concentration.
validation: Predictive capability was evaluated against a separate fed-batch experiment with lower initial glucose and glutamine and feeding twice daily.

Sup B: lopezmeza_2016 · Using simple models to describe the kinetics of growth, glucose consumption, and monoclonal antibody formation in naive and infliximab producer CHO cells
The model describes growth, glucose use, and infliximab-biosimilar production by native and recombinant CHO-S cells. It combines first-order growth during the exponential phase with a threshold-modified Monod growth relationship, a cell-yield description of glucose consumption, and a Luedeking–Piret description of antibody formation. The authors developed it using batch cultures in shake flasks at different initial glucose concentrations and temperatures, then evaluated its product-formation description in instrumented batch and fed-batch bioreactors. Cell, glucose, lactate, and active antibody concentrations were measured daily. The authors present the simple kinetic models as tools for understanding and characterizing cell-culture processes, and for applications such as monitoring, control, and optimization.
availability: The paper does not report a code or data repository.
cell lines: The model concerns native CHO-S cells and an in-house engineered recombinant CHO-S clone producing an infliximab biosimilar.
data processing: Cell and glucose profiles during exponential growth were fitted with second-order polynomials and differentiated to estimate growth and glucose-consumption rates.
data processing: For antibody-production analysis, viable-cell profiles were fitted with a sixth-order polynomial and differentiated to estimate cell-growth rates.
equipment: Instrumented bioreactor experiments used 1.6-L vessels with a 1.0-L working volume and were conducted only with recombinant cells.
equipment: Shake-flask batch cultures used 125-mL flasks with a 30-mL working volume.
estimation: For 37 °C recombinant batch data, the authors iteratively adjusted selected growth, yield, and production parameters while holding the threshold and one production coefficient fixed.
estimation: The authors selected the product-formation coefficients by fitting multiple cell-density and antibody-production data sets and numerically integrating the model.
estimation: The growth-kinetic parameters were obtained using Lineweaver–Burk linearization, and a linear regression was accepted only when its r² exceeded 0.97.
feeding: Shake-flask batch experiments tested initial glucose concentrations of 1.2, 2.4, 3.6, and 4.8 g/L.
feeding: The methods describe fed-batch operation with five intermittent additions of feed, each 10% of the initial culture volume, starting on day 1, and a temperature reduction on day 7.
fit: The authors report that the product-formation parameters fitted shake-flask data over initial substrate concentrations from 2.4 to 4.5 g/L.
growth: The authors treat cell growth as first-order in cell concentration during at least the initial portion of exponential growth.
growth: The fitted Monod parameters for recombinant cells were reported to change little with temperature, whereas those for naive cells changed with temperature.
growth: The growth relationship is Monod-type but includes a nonzero glucose threshold below which growth is not observed.
lactate: Lactate was measured and discussed, but the model laws described in the paper do not include a lactate balance or lactate effect.
limitations: A single pair of product-formation coefficients did not describe all the 37 °C batch data sets, and the authors suggest lactate inhibition as a possible model improvement.
measurement: Cell density and viability were measured by trypan-blue exclusion using a Guava easyCyte flow cytometer.
measurement: Glucose and lactate were measured by HPLC with refractive-index detection using an Aminex HPX 87H column and 5 mM sulfuric acid mobile phase.
measurement: The antibody assay quantified active monoclonal antibody in culture samples by ELISA.
measurement: The measured time series included viable cell density, glucose, lactic acid, and monoclonal antibody concentrations.
medium: Cultures used CD Opti CHO medium supplemented with 8 mM glutamine.
model size: The paper does not give a consolidated count of model states, equations, or estimated parameters.
model type: The authors characterize their approach as simple, unstructured kinetic modeling.
operation: Bioreactor batch runs lasted 10 days and fed-batch runs lasted 20 days, with duplicate cultures and daily sampling.
operation: Bioreactor cultures were agitated at 80 rpm and supplied with 2 standard L/h of gas to maintain dissolved oxygen at 40% saturation.
operation: Shake-flask cultures were inoculated at about 2 × 10⁵ viable cells/mL and incubated at 33 or 37 °C, 125 rpm, and 8% CO₂.
prior models: The authors contrast their approach with earlier recombinant-cell studies using structured kinetic, logistic, Monte Carlo, and regression models, including Sandadi et al. 2011, Goudar et al. 2009, Xing et al. 2010, and Farges et al. 2008.
prior models: The paper places its growth model alongside Monod-like and logistic hybridoma models, Monod and metabolic-flux models, and dynamic metabolic models for nonproducing CHO cells.
prior models: The product-formation model is identified as a Luedeking–Piret model, citing Luedeking and Piret 1959.
product: Antibody formation is represented with a Luedeking–Piret model, combining growth-associated and viable-cell-associated production.
product: The authors describe production by this recombinant line as mixed-mode, with formation related to both growth rate and viable-cell concentration.
sampling: Shake-flask cultures were run in triplicate with daily sampling and were stopped after 7 days for recombinant cells or 10 days for naive cells.
scope: The authors state that the proposed product-formation parameters fit experimental data sets in the range of 31–33 °C.
substrate use: The authors found that the cell/substrate yield coefficient varied with glucose concentration rather than remaining constant.
substrate use: The model relates glucose consumption to cell growth through a cell/substrate yield coefficient.
use: The authors propose simple kinetic models as practical tools for process characterization, online monitoring, process control, and optimization.
validation: For fed-batch validation, the paper describes a representative instrumented run with a temperature shift from 37 to 33 °C on day 7.
validation: The authors also applied the batch-derived kinetic parameter set to fed-batch cultures, where they report that the model fit the measured data.
validation: The product-formation description was tested on recombinant-cell batch cultures in instrumented bioreactors, and the authors report a good fit using the shake-flask parameter set.

answer.summary: A and B both model mammalian cell growth and monoclonal-antibody production, but A describes IgG1-producing hybridomas with intracellular synthesis detail, whereas B uses simple kinetics for native and recombinant CHO-S cells.

differences.in_b: Simple unstructured kinetics using growth, cell/substrate yield, and Luedeking–Piret product-formation descriptions

differences.in_a: Batch and pulse-fed-batch cultures in Erlenmeyer flasks
differences.in_b: Batch shake-flask cultures and recombinant-cell batch and fed-batch bioreactor runs
